\[
\hat G = \hat G^{bl} + \alpha\, \Delta_R,
\quad
\hat R = \hat R^{bl} + \beta\, \Delta_G \text{ (at green)},
\quad
\hat R = \hat R^{bl} + \gamma\, \Delta_B \text{ (at blue)},
\qquad \alpha = \tfrac{1}{2},\ \beta = \tfrac{5}{8},\ \gamma = \tfrac{3}{4}
\]

The formula shows the default parameter values.

where

- \(\hat G^{bl}, \hat R^{bl}\): The bilinear estimates
- \(\Delta_R, \Delta_G, \Delta_B\): Laplacians of the channel known at the pixel
- \(\alpha, \beta, \gamma\): The weights of the corrections

The hat with bl is the bilinear estimate. For G it is the mean of the 4 axial neighbors. For R or B at a green pixel it is the mean of the 2 nearest samples. For R at B or B at R it is the mean of the 4 diagonal samples. Malvar, He and Cutler add a Laplacian of the channel that is known at the pixel. Delta_R is the red value minus the mean of the 4 red samples 2 pixels away. Delta_G is a 9-point Laplacian of green and Delta_B a 5-point Laplacian of blue. Blue is estimated like red. They chose alpha, beta and gamma for the smallest mean squared error on the Kodak image set, rounded to dyadic fractions. The result is eight 5 x 5 filters with weights in eighths, as Getreuer's IPOL article shows them. Bilinear is the same without the correction.
